title: Prompt anchoring & stream safety: experiment PRD
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact PRD + experiment plan for a new Hosted API surface were calling "prompt anchoring". Goal: make incremental streaming safe and predictable for client tool-handshakes and for structured/opaque outputs while keeping SDK ergonomics simple for product teams.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Many apps rely on partial streaming responses but struggle to reconcile tool-calls, structured JSON fragments and client-side replays when partial tokens are emitted.
- Current streaming semantics place the burden on clients to diff and guess commit boundaries; tool invocations can race or be invoked multiple times under poor network conditions.
- Structured output schemas are brittle when a model switches phrasing mid-stream or when a partial object is emitted; consumers either block for full output or implement fragile parsers.

Hypothesis:
If the Hosted API surfaces an "anchor" primitive (small, monotonic markers embedded in the stream) plus a light client-side prefetch/backpressure protocol, then:
- Tool-calls will be invoked exactly-once (or have a deterministic retry contract) despite partial streams and reconnects.
- Consumers of structured outputs will be able to accept opaque anchors and assemble a valid object without needing to reparse text diffs.
- SDK ergonomics can remain minimal: we add a thin event API (onAnchor, onPartial, onCommit) and opt-in heuristics for prefetching to reduce tail latency.

Primary users & personas:
- Mobile app teams using hosted streaming for chat with tool integrations (e.g., code execution, search).
- Web editors relying on incremental structured output (document JSON, patch lists).
- Platform teams embedding Redwood as a predictable inference surface for third-party microservices.

Success metrics (measurable):
- Reduction in duplicate tool-call incidents observed in SLO logs: target 90% reduction for participating customers in first 8 weeks.
- Reduction in parser-error alerts for structured-output consumers: target 70% lower than baseline on pilot prompts.
- SDK adoption: pilot 3 internal apps, 2 external partners using anchor-enabled SDK within quarter.
- Latency impact: median token latency change <= +5ms; p95 <= +30ms for anchored streams.

Principles and constraints:
- Backwards-compatible: streams without anchors must continue to work unchanged.
- Anchors must be small, non-semantic and safe to ignore by un-updated clients.
- Avoid heavyweight server-side coordination or persistent per-session state beyond a lightweight sequence counter.
- Tool invocation guarantees should be explicit (exactly-once preferred, at-least-once with idempotency token acceptable).

Proposed primitives (surface level):
1) Anchor token ("anchor_id")
- Server emits textual frames interleaved with special meta frames carrying an anchor_id.
- Anchor is monotonic per session (anchor_1, anchor_2, ...) and references a stable checkpoint of the stream state (KV of prompt + token offset).
- Anchor frames optionally include a short schema-hint (e.g., "json-part", "tool-call-ready") - small labels only.

2) Commit frame (finalization)
- When a logical unit (tool output, JSON object) is complete, server emits a commit for the anchor id (commit:anchor_5).
- Commit indicates the unit is safe to persist/act on. If a client sees the commit it may trigger side-effects (apply patch, call webhook).

3) Anchor-ack / client hedging
- Clients may send lightweight anchor-ack over the streaming socket to confirm receipt; a lack of ack triggers SDK backoff/ hedging behavior described below.

4) Idempotency token for tool-calls
- When stream indicates a tool-call, the server attaches a tool_call_id that clients should pass through to the external tool bridge so retries are safe.

SDK ergonomics proposal (minimal surface):
- New optional streaming callbacks: onPartial(text), onAnchor(anchorId, hint), onCommit(anchorId), onToolCall(tool_call_id, metadata).
- Default behavior: SDK buffers until onCommit for structured fragments, exposes a convenience method applyWhenCommitted(anchorId, callback).
- Prefetch setting: prefetch_strategy = [none | minimal | opportunistic]. Minimal waits for anchor then prefetches small supporting context; opportunistic prefetches predicted tool input before commit (hedged, cancelable).
- Backpressure: SDK exposes setBackpressure(target_tokens) to hint server batching and reduce overshoot on mobile.

Server-side behavior and guarantees:
- Anchors are persisted in ephemeral session metadata: (session_id -> latest_anchor_id -> token_offset, schema_hint, tool_call_id). Lightweight, GC after session end + 1 minute.
- When a reconnect occurs, client can request resume(anchor_id) to receive from the last checkpoint rather than the beginning; server uses anchor_id mapping to compute delta.
- Tool-call semantics: server ensures a tool_call frame is only emitted after the model has reached a stable predicate; server will not mark commit until tool results are included or a configured fallback is used.

Structured output strategy (opaque anchors):
- Instead of enforcing well-formed JSON in the raw token stream, we allow the model to emit opaque JSON fragments wrapped with anchors.
- The SDK reconstructs by concatenating anchored fragments in anchor order and performing a single parse at commit time. This avoids partial-parse failures and complex diffing.
- For very large outputs, anchors can carry incremental checksums to validate continuity.

Tool calling / safety & hedging model:
- Tool-call frames include: tool_call_id, canonical_input_digest, suggested_timeout_ms.
- Clients can choose immediate invocation on seeing tool_call frame (optimistic) or wait for commit (conservative). Suggest opt-in policy 'invoke_on_anchor' with default false to avoid accidental side-effects.
- To reduce tail latency, SDK opportunistic prefetch may call read-only tools (search) with cancelable requests; SDK exposes cancelHook tied to tool_call_id.

Migration and compatibility:
- Existing SDKs ignore anchor meta-frames and treat stream as text -> compatible.
- New SDKs will default to conservative commit-on-commit behavior; opt-in flags needed to enable optimistic tool invocation or opportunistic prefetch.
- Provide a server-side toggle per-customer to enable anchored streams for pilot customers.

Operational considerations:
- Observability: emit metrics: anchor_emit_rate, anchor_commit_latency, duplicate_tool_call_count, anchor_resume_rate.
- Billing: anchored streams are billed same as normal tokens; additional metadata frames negligible.
- Storage: ephemeral small index per session; plan capacity for 50k sessions and average 4 anchors/session for pilot.

Experiment plan (8 weeks):
Week 0-2: implement anchor meta-frame + SDK prototype (Node + iOS) with minimal callbacks. Smoke tests with internal apps.
Week 3-4: run end-to-end pilot with internal Search-in-Chat and Code Runner. Measure duplicate tool calls and parser errors.
Week 5-6: iterate fallback policies (invoke_on_anchor default off, provide opt-in) and opportunistic prefetch heuristics.
Week 7-8: extend resume flow and validation checksums; prepare rollout checklist for customer enablement.

Open questions / risks:
- How much extra complexity will SDKs adopt vs. teams ignoring anchors and continuing fragile parsing?
- Is anchor persistence a target for abuse if customers attempt to store large session histories? (limit to tiny mapping, GC aggressively).
- Can opportunistic prefetching cause excessive non-idempotent tool usage? Mitigate via default conservative policies and explicit opt-in for mutable tool calls.

Appendix: quick example interaction (sketch)
Server stream frames (ordered):
- partial: "Generating plan...
- anchor: {id:anchor_3, hint:json-part}", partial: "{"ops": [
- partial: "  {"op": "edit", "text": "fix"}", anchor: {id:anchor_4, hint:json-part}", commit: {anchor_4}
Client SDK behavior:
- onAnchor(anchor_3): buffer fragment into fragmentMap[anchor_3] = "{"ops": ["
- onAnchor(anchor_4): append fragment; onCommit(anchor_4): concatenate fragmentMap in order -> parse JSON -> call applyWhenCommitted -> app invokes patch once.

Next steps (short):
- Sync with runtime/serving team to validate low-cost anchor emission in realtime runtime (impact on kernel selection negligible).
- Build Node + iOS SDK prototypes and a debug tool to visualize anchors.
- Create pilot enablement doc and customer-facing changelog language that clarifies anchor opt-in behavior.

Notes to reviewers: this is an exploratory PRD. Focus review on whether the anchor semantics are simple enough for SDKs and whether commit/ack tradeoffs are acceptable for canary customers.
